mcqs.q: Normal hemostasis depends on the interaction of:
opts: The blood-vessel wall, platelets and the coagulation cascade
mcqs.explain: Hemostasis depends on the interaction between the vessel wall, platelets and the coagulation cascade.

mcqs.q: Primary hemostasis culminates in the formation of:
opts: A platelet plug (adhesion via von Willebrand factor)
mcqs.explain: Primary hemostasis forms the platelet plug — vasoconstriction then platelet adhesion (via vWF) and activation.

mcqs.q: Disorders of PRIMARY hemostasis characteristically cause:
opts: Immediate, superficial bleeding such as petechiae and gingival bleeding
mcqs.explain: Primary (vessel/platelet/vWF) defects cause immediate superficial bleeding — petechiae, purpura, gingival bleeding, epistaxis — with a prolonged bleeding time.

mcqs.q: Which substance is formed by SECONDARY hemostasis?
mcqs.explain: Secondary hemostasis is the coagulation cascade that generates fibrin to strengthen the platelet plug.

mcqs.q: The main (extrinsic) pathway of coagulation is initiated by:
opts: Tissue factor (factor III) combining with factor VII to activate factor X
mcqs.explain: The extrinsic (main) pathway begins with tissue factor (III) at the injury site; the tissue factor–factor VII complex activates factor X.

mcqs.q: In the common pathway, thrombin acts to:
mcqs.explain: Activated factor X converts prothrombin to thrombin, which then cleaves fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh.

mcqs.q: Disorders of SECONDARY hemostasis (clotting factors) typically cause:
opts: Delayed, deep bleeding such as haematomas and haemarthrosis
mcqs.explain: Clotting-factor defects (e.g. hemophilia) cause delayed, deep bleeding into muscles and joints; superficial bleeding stops normally at first.

mcqs.q: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is:
opts: An autosomal-dominant vascular dysplasia with telangiectasia and AV malformations
mcqs.explain: HHT is autosomal dominant; vascular dysplasia produces mucocutaneous telangiectasia and arteriovenous malformations.

mcqs.q: In a patient with HHT, which dental precaution is advised?
opts: Avoid regional LA blocks because of deep-bleeding risk
mcqs.explain: Regional LA blocks are avoided (risk of deep bleeding); antibiotic prophylaxis is considered when a pulmonary AVM coexists (cerebral abscess risk).

mcqs.q: Immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is due to:
mcqs.explain: ITP is autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction (sometimes linked to HIV/HCV); splenomegaly is rare.

mcqs.q: The first-line treatment of ITP is:
mcqs.explain: Corticosteroids are first-line; second-line options include IVIg, splenectomy (after vaccination) and immunosuppressants.

mcqs.q: A regional LA block injection is considered safe when the platelet count is above:
mcqs.explain: Regional blocks need platelets >30 × 10⁹/L; dento-alveolar surgery >50; major surgery >75 × 10⁹/L.

mcqs.q: Which platelet level is considered safe for MAJOR surgical procedures?
mcqs.explain: Major surgery requires platelet levels above 75 × 10⁹/L; 50 is enough for dento-alveolar surgery and 30 for a block.

mcqs.q: Hemophilia A is caused by a deficiency of:
mcqs.explain: Hemophilia A is an X-linked deficiency of factor VIII, affecting males; it is commoner than hemophilia B.

mcqs.q: The characteristic laboratory finding in hemophilia A is:
opts: Prolonged APTT with a normal PT and low factor VIII
Prolonged PT with a normal APTT
A raised bleeding time with normal APTT
mcqs.explain: Hemophilia A prolongs the APTT (intrinsic pathway) with a normal PT/INR and a low factor VIII level.

mcqs.q: The most common intra-oral bleeding site in hemophilia is the:
mcqs.explain: Bleeding sites in hemophilia: labial frenum 60%, tongue 23%, buccal mucosa 17%, gingiva/palate 3%.

mcqs.q: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) differs from hemophilia A in that:
opts: It is due to factor IX deficiency and desmopressin does not work
It is due to factor VIII deficiency
mcqs.explain: Hemophilia B is a factor IX deficiency; management is like A but uses factor IX and desmopressin is ineffective.

mcqs.q: von Willebrand disease is best described as:
opts: The commonest hereditary coagulation disorder, autosomal dominant, affecting both sexes
An X-linked disorder of males only
mcqs.explain: vWD is the most common hereditary coagulation disorder, autosomal dominant, affecting males and females; vWF aids platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII.

mcqs.q: Which LA technique is preferred over a regional block in severe hemophilia (without factor cover)?
mcqs.explain: Regional blocks, lingual and floor-of-mouth injections (≈80% haematoma) are avoided without factor VIII; intraligamentary/intraosseous injections are safer alternatives.

mcqs.q: For dental extractions in severe hemophilia A, factor VIII should be raised to about:
mcqs.explain: Extractions need factor VIII at 50–75% (75–100% for maxillofacial surgery), with tranexamic acid cover and local haemostatic measures.

mcqs.q: For pain control in hemophilia, the preferred analgesic is:
mcqs.explain: Paracetamol or codeine/paracetamol is suitable; NSAIDs and aspirin are avoided as they worsen bleeding.

mcqs.q: Preventive dentistry should be started as early as possible (when teeth begin to erupt) in:
mcqs.explain: In hemophilia, prevention is paramount; preventive dentistry begins as the teeth erupt to avoid invasive treatment later.

mcqs.q: A patient on long-term anticoagulant therapy needs an extraction. The correct approach is:
opts: Do not stop the anticoagulant; check INR and use local haemostatic measures
Stop the anticoagulant at any time it is convenient
Use a regional nerve block routinely
mcqs.explain: Anticoagulation should not be stopped (risk of thrombotic death); check INR, avoid IM injections and regional blocks, and control bleeding locally.

mcqs.q: According to UKMI guidance, dental surgery in primary care should NOT be done when the INR is:
mcqs.explain: UKMI recommends no dental procedure in primary care if INR > 4; an INR is checked within 24–72 h of the procedure.

mcqs.q: The immediate anticoagulant effect of heparin can be reversed with:
mcqs.explain: Heparin acts for only 4–6 h; in an emergency it is reversed with IV protamine sulfate (1 mg per 100 IU heparin).

mcqs.q: In liver disease, the bleeding tendency arises because the liver fails to make:
opts: Vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X)
mcqs.explain: Liver failure impairs synthesis of vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors, prolonging PT/INR; treat with FFP and vitamin K.

mcqs.q: Vascular purpura (e.g. senile purpura) characteristically:
opts: Bleeds immediately after trauma but stops within 24–48 hours, with normal platelets
Has a very low platelet count
mcqs.explain: Vascular purpura rarely bleeds seriously; bleeding starts immediately after trauma and stops within 24–48 hours, with normal platelet count and function.

mcqs.q: Which absorbable local agent can be placed in a socket to assist clotting?
mcqs.explain: Absorbable haemostatic agents — oxidised regenerated cellulose (Surgicel) or collagen (Instat/Avitene) — are placed in the socket to assist clotting.

mcqs.q: Prolonged post-operative bleeding is defined when bleeding:
opts: Continues for 12 hours, makes the patient return, or causes a large haematoma
Is just a small ooze for an hour
mcqs.explain: Prolonged bleeding = continues ≥12 h, causes the patient to return, or produces a large haematoma/ecchymosis — prompting local measures and a search for a systemic cause.

saqs.q: Describe the three phases of hemostasis.
saqs.a: Primary: vasoconstriction + platelet plug (vWF adhesion). Secondary: coagulation cascade (intrinsic/extrinsic/common) forming fibrin. Tertiary (fibrinolysis): t-PA → plasmin breaks down the clot.

saqs.q: Contrast the bleeding pattern of primary vs secondary hemostatic disorders.
saqs.a: Primary (vessel/platelet/vWF): immediate, superficial bleeding (petechiae, gingival, epistaxis), prolonged bleeding time. Secondary (clotting factors): delayed, deep bleeding (haematomas, haemarthrosis).

saqs.q: Give the platelet-count thresholds for dental procedures.
saqs.a: Regional LA block >30 × 10⁹/L; dento-alveolar surgery >50 × 10⁹/L; major surgery >75 × 10⁹/L.

saqs.q: Describe hemophilia A: inheritance, defect, diagnosis.
saqs.a: X-linked deficiency of factor VIII, affecting males. Deep bleeding into muscles/joints. Diagnosis: prolonged APTT, normal PT/INR, low factor VIII.

saqs.q: Compare hemophilia B and von Willebrand disease.
saqs.a: Hemophilia B (Christmas disease): factor IX deficiency; desmopressin ineffective. vWD: commonest hereditary coagulation disorder, autosomal dominant, both sexes; vWF aids platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII; treat with desmopressin + vWF replacement.

saqs.q: Outline the dental management of a hemophilia patient.
saqs.a: Prevention first; consult haematologist. Avoid regional blocks/IM injections (use intraligamentary). Cover: mild → desmopressin/antifibrinolytics; severe → factor VIII 50–75% + tranexamic acid. Pain: paracetamol, avoid NSAIDs/aspirin.

saqs.q: State the rules for managing a warfarinised patient (UKMI).
saqs.a: Do not stop anticoagulation (thrombotic death). Check INR within 24–72 h; no surgery in primary care if INR > 4; prefer intraligamentary injections; control bleeding with local measures; warfarin may resume the evening of surgery.
